Laser printers are consistently more reliable than inkjet printers, based on Consumer Reports' surveys.

Consumer Reports' surveys, based on 69,886 individual printers purchased between 2016 and 2024, indicate significant differences in reliability among printer brands and types, particularly for inkjet printers.

Many inkjet printers are designed for the lowest possible selling price, often leading to lower long-term reliability due to complex internal machinery (motors, pulleys, gears) that can fail. [Consumer Reports]
Initial savings on inexpensive inkjet printers are often offset several times over by high ink costs during the first few years of ownership. [Consumer Reports]
Consumer Reports rarely recommends traditional inkjet printers due to their hidden costs and reliability problems, which lead to low owner satisfaction ratings.
Solid alternatives to traditional inkjets include laser printers and tank-style inkjets. [Consumer Reports]
Inkjet printers are suitable if you don't print a lot and need a combination of text, graphics, and photos (especially in color), but be aware of their drawbacks. [Consumer Reports]

report.summary: The strongest evidence points to Brother and Epson, with Brother leading for simple, reliable home document printing and Epson leading when you want ink-tank economics or photo quality. Consumer Reports and PCMag both caution that traditional cartridge inkjets are often a bad long-term deal because of ink cost and reliability, while laser and tank printers are the safer home-buying paths. Several older models in the notes are now stale or likely discontinued, so this report focuses on current 2026 recommendations supported by recent expert testing.

report.summary: After reviewing current expert sources, the best printer for home use depends on your printing volume and need for color. Laser printers from Brother offer exceptional reliability and fast, crisp text output for monochrome document-centric households. For those who print photos or need color occasionally, tank-style inkjet printers from Canon and Epson eliminate expensive cartridges, delivering very low per-page costs. Budget-conscious buyers can find capable monochrome lasers and color ink tanks under $200, while full-featured color laser all-in-one units suit demanding home-office users but command a higher price.

report.summary: For a typical home in 2026, a color laser all-in-one is the safest pick — laser printers are meaningfully more reliable than inkjets per Consumer Reports' 2016-2024 survey data, and the Brother MFC-L3780CDW is PCMag's Editors' Choice with a 4.5 rating. If you print only documents, a budget monochrome laser like the HP LaserJet M209d ($109) or Wirecutter's top home pick, the Brother DCP-L2640DW, will outlast any cheap inkjet. For photos, the Epson Expression Photo XP-8800 is the standout; for low-volume color on a budget, the Canon Pixma G3270 MegaTank avoids the cartridge trap that sinks most sub-$150 inkjets.

products.name: Brother MFC-L3780CDW
pros: PCMag Editors' Choice with a 4.5 'Outstanding' rating, repeatedly named the top all-in-one color laser by hands-on testers
Color laser output is smudge- and fade-resistant and dramatically more reliable long-term than inkjet per Consumer Reports survey data
Fast print speeds confirmed by RTINGS hands-on testing; also flagged as a quicker alternative to the Canon Color imageCLASS MF665Cdw
Brother is Consumer Reports' top-rated brand for printer reliability in their 2016-2024 dataset of 69,886 printers
cons: Sticker price of ~$570 is steep for casual home use — this is a home-office purchase, not a casual-use purchase
Larger and heavier than mono lasers or inkjet AIOs; needs a real spot on a desk, not a shelf
Toner cartridges, while cheap per page, are a larger upfront outlay than a $109 entry-level laser
products.verdict: The strongest current pick for a home that prints, scans, and copies in color with any regularity. Hands-on testing by PCMag (Editors' Choice, 4.5) and RTINGS backs the speed claims, and Brother's reliability lead in Consumer Reports' data reduces the usual laser-printer risk. Worth the $570 if you print a few hundred pages a month; overkill otherwise.
products.best_for: Home and home-office users who print/copy/scan in color regularly and want a printer that will still work in 5 years

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW
pros: Wirecutter's current #1 pick for best home printer, praised as 'reliable, cheap to buy and run, and simple to operate'
Monochrome laser means no dried-out print heads and dramatically lower per-page cost than any inkjet
Brother's brand-level reliability advantage carries over from the MFC line per Consumer Reports survey data
cons: Monochrome only — no color printing at all, so photo/graphics jobs are out
$380 is meaningfully more than the HP LaserJet M209d for what is essentially a no-frills mono laser
No fax (which most homes don't need) but also lacks the MFC-L3780CDW's larger paper capacity
products.verdict: Wirecutter's #1 home pick, and the right answer for homes that print mostly documents. It sacrifices color and a few hundred dollars of your wallet compared to the MFC-L3780CDW, in exchange for proven reliability and the lowest ongoing cost in this roundup. Best for: families with school-age kids printing assignments.

pros: PCMag Editors' Choice with a 4.0 'Excellent' rating, currently $109 at Amazon (down from $159) — cheapest credible laser pick in the roundup

Simple, single-function design that just prints reliably — no scanner/copier to break
cons: Mono only, no scanning or copying — you give up the 'all-in-one' flexibility most home users actually want

Doesn't include duplex printing at this price tier on every configuration
products.verdict: If all you need is a cheap, reliable, no-drama printer for documents, this is the one PCMag put an Editors' Choice on. The $109 street price is the floor for a credible home laser. Skip it if you need color or a scanner — buy the DCP-L2640DW or MFC-L3780CDW instead.
products.best_for: Minimalist buyers who only need to print black-and-white documents on a budget

products.name: Canon Pixma G3270 Wireless MegaTank All-In-One

All-in-one (print/scan/copy) plus wireless for $159 — the best feature-per-dollar in the roundup

Slower than every laser on this list; not appropriate for printing 500-page documents
Photo quality is decent but not in the Epson XP-8800 class; better for schoolwork than for a photo hobbyist
products.verdict: The right answer for low-volume, mixed-color, budget-conscious homes. MegaTank ink economics finally make a sub-$200 inkjet defensible. Just commit to printing at least once a week, or you'll get the same clogged-head failure mode that sinks every cartridge-based inkjet.
products.best_for: Low-volume home users who need an all-in-one for under $200 and will print at least weekly

products.verdict: Buy this only if you actually print photos — it's the best home photo printer PCMag has tested and earns the 4.5 Editors' Choice on that specific job. report.summary: Based on hands-on testing by PCMag, Consumer Reports, and RTINGS, the best home printers balance cost-per-page, reliability, and print quality. Laser printers dominate for text and speed; tank-style inkjets excel for color and photos while minimizing ink costs. Brother and Epson lead in reliability; avoid cheap traditional inkjets due to hidden cartridge costs and poor long-term satisfaction.

cons: High upfront cost at $569.98, though justified by low cost-per-page over time
Larger footprint than single-function printers; requires dedicated desk space
products.verdict: PCMag's top pick for color laser printing combines speed, quality, and reliability. Ideal for households that print frequently and need color output; the high upfront cost is offset by low toner expenses and proven durability over 3+ years.
